query: How do graph-based methods compare to tabular approaches for real-time credit card fraud detection?
title: Graph vs. Tabular Methods for Real-Time Credit Card Fraud Detection
synthesis:
Graph-based fraud detection systems model the relational structure of financial transactions, allowing them to identify coordinated fraud rings and multi-hop collusion patterns that are invisible to account-level tabular classifiers. [[xu2022graph]] demonstrates that a heterogeneous GNN operating on an account–merchant bipartite graph achieves 12–18 pp higher AUC-PR than gradient-boosted tabular models on high-value transaction sets, at the cost of higher infrastructure complexity and a 48-hour graph lookback requirement.

Tabular approaches, by contrast, excel in regulatory environments where model explainability is mandated. [[bolton2001statistical]] shows that velocity features over rolling time windows retain 85% of the discriminative signal achievable by neural models while providing transparent, auditable decision rules compatible with GDPR Article 22. In practice, many production systems combine both paradigms: a fast logistic-regression scorer for real-time decisioning and a GNN-based batch job that flags accounts for investigation.

The key trade-offs are latency versus expressiveness and interpretability versus recall. Graph models require graph materialization and multi-hop neighborhood sampling, pushing p99 latency to 78–120 ms even on GPU hardware, whereas tabular models can score transactions in under 5 ms on commodity CPUs. The choice between approaches should be driven by the fraud typology mix: card-present counterfeit fraud skews toward tabular velocity signals, while first-party bust-out and account-takeover schemes benefit most from graph topology features.
